preamble.summary: Habakkuk 2:4 — 'the righteous shall live by his faith / faithfulness' — is one of the single most theologically loaded verses in the Hebrew Bible for Christian history. The NT quotes it three times (Romans 1:17, Galatians 3:11, Hebrews 10:38) and each citation uses the LXX wording in a slightly different form. Habakkuk 1:5 is also cited by Paul in Acts 13:41. LXX Habakkuk's text-critical situation is unusually rich: the Nahal Hever Greek Minor Prophets scroll (8ḤevXIIgr, 1st c. BCE–CE) preserves a pre-Christian revision of LXX Habakkuk that sometimes agrees more closely with MT, and NT citations occasionally align with this revision rather than with standard Rahlfs.
preamble.notable_variants: Habakkuk 2:4 in its various forms: MT ('the righteous shall live by his [the righteous's] faith'), LXX ('the righteous shall live by my [God's] faithfulness'), 1QpHab ('by their faith/faithfulness in the Teacher of Righteousness'), NT (Paul drops the pronoun; Hebrews keeps God as the agent). Each form carries a distinct theological freight.
preamble.theological_legacy: Habakkuk 2:4 in its Pauline-LXX form is the scriptural motto of the Protestant Reformation ('the just shall live by faith'). Luther's discovery of iustus ex fide vivit as the heart of the gospel is a discovery of LXX Habakkuk mediated through Vulgate and Paul. The verse's afterlife across two millennia is disproportionate to its brief original context.

renderings.mt_reading: רְאוּ בַגּוֹיִם וְהַבִּיטוּ וְהִתַּמְּהוּ תְּמָהוּ כִּי־פֹעַל פֹּעֵל בִּימֵיכֶם
renderings.lxx_reading: ἴδετε οἱ καταφρονηταί καὶ ἐπιβλέψατε καὶ θαυμάσατε θαυμάσια καὶ ἀφανίσθητε διότι ἔργον ἐγὼ ἐργάζομαι ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις ὑμῶν
renderings.mt_rendering: Look among the nations and observe — be utterly astounded!
renderings.lxx_rendering: Look, O despisers, and behold, and wonder at wonders, and vanish — for I am working a work in your days
notes: LXX has hoi kataphronētai ('O despisers') for Hebrew ba-goyim ('among the nations'). The two Hebrew consonants b-g-w-y-m can be vocalized either way, and the LXX reads bogedim ('treacherous ones, despisers'). This is a significant variant.

Acts 13:41 quotes this verse in its LXX form — idete hoi kataphronētai — as Paul's warning to the Antioch synagogue. Paul uses the LXX reading 'O despisers' rather than the MT reading 'among the nations,' which turns the verse from a universal-astonishment oracle into a specific warning to unbelieving Jewish hearers.
This is a clear case where the NT quotation depends specifically on the LXX's vocalization choice.

renderings.lxx_reading: ὅτι ἐρχόμενος ἥξει καὶ οὐ μὴ χρονίσῃ
renderings.mt_rendering: it will surely come; it will not delay
renderings.lxx_rendering: for the one coming will come and will not delay
notes: Hebrews 10:37 cites this verse in LXX form — ho erchomenos hēxei kai ou chronisei ('the one who is coming will come, and will not delay') — and interpretively identifies the 'one coming' (ho erchomenos) with Jesus Christ. The LXX's masculine participle 'the one coming' (read as personal) rather than Hebrew's neuter 'it' (the vision) enables this Christological reading.

The LXX's ho erchomenos phrasing is one of the NT's standard Messianic titles (Matt 11:3 'are you the one who is to come?' Mark 11:9, John 1:27, etc.). Habakkuk 2:3 is the textual origin of this Messianic expectation-title in its Greek form.

renderings.lxx_reading: ὁ δὲ δίκαιος ἐκ πίστεώς μου ζήσεται (some MSS: ἐκ πίστεως ζήσεται)
renderings.mt_rendering: the righteous shall live by his faithfulness
renderings.lxx_rendering: the righteous shall live by my faith (some MSS: the righteous shall live by faith)
notes: The three main textual forms of this verse each frame the verse's theology differently. MT has 'his (the righteous person's) faithfulness' — the righteous live by their own covenant fidelity. Standard LXX (A-text) has 'my (God's) faithfulness' — the righteous live by God's covenant faithfulness. A shorter LXX form and the Nahal Hever revision drop the possessive pronoun entirely — 'by faith.'

Paul in Romans 1:17 and Galatians 3:11 cites the short form without the pronoun: ho dikaios ek pisteōs zēsetai. This version — 'the righteous by faith shall live' — is neither MT (his) nor standard LXX (my). Paul may be working from a textual tradition closer to the Nahal Hever revision, or he may be deliberately deleting the pronoun to open the verse up theologically.

Hebrews 10:38 cites the verse with the pronoun — ho dikaios mou ek pisteōs zēsetai — 'my righteous one shall live by faith.' Hebrews's form is unique among NT citations and may reflect yet another Greek textual tradition.

The three NT citations (Romans, Galatians, Hebrews) and the three OT forms (MT, standard LXX, short LXX) make Habakkuk 2:4 the single most complex case-study in NT-OT textual relations. Every theology of 'justification by faith' that traces itself to this verse should know that it does so through a web of textual choices.
